## Summary

The songs people recognise fastest have choruses built from common cells and plain intervals. Our choruses do the opposite: they repeat themselves less than at least 94% of real choruses their length.

- **v7** has more hook theory than any other area: Module 23, Window 17, the money note, the quotable line. It never tested a hook against recognition, and its strength indicators reward an unusual interval.

- **The research** that measured memory (Hooked, 1,715 sections of 321 songs) found the voice, typical sound and melody, and repetition made sections recognisable. Distinctiveness did not. Listeners name a familiar song by about the 6th note, helped by long notes, downbeats and phrase boundaries more than by pitch.

- **Measured on 22,407 Hooktheory sections:** a chorus is mainly higher than its verse (67% of songs, +1.5 semitones). It is only a little more repetitive and no more typical. The 14 fastest-recognised songs' choruses sit at the 81st percentile for typical cells, the 33rd for interval variety and the 27th for surprise.

- **Titles (156 Billboard hits):** sung in the chorus in 87% of songs with one, about twice per chorus and 8 times per song, in the chorus's first line more often than its last (40% against 28%), first heard at about 39 seconds.

- **Songs 52 to 56:** every chorus at the 1st to 6th percentile for self-repetition; in songs 54 to 56 the verse repeats more than the chorus. Song 56 never sings its title.

- **For v8:** six rules (section 5). Score typicality instead of an unusual interval, make the chorus repeat its own cell, place the title as hits do, carry identity in rhythm, keep each section's job, and test both recognition and singing back.

Eleven new lines of work came from the bibliographies and arXiv (section 3). The strongest next one is YouTube's replay curve, a moment-by-moment listener outcome.

## 1. What Luthier v7 does now

v7 has more hook theory than any other area, but it has never measured a hook against what a hook is for: being recognised and recalled. Every test so far used the chart, weeks on the chart or views, and found almost nothing. The recognition data that could measure the hook itself (Hooked on Music) was named in Window 63 as not reachable from the build.

|Rule in v7|What it does|What it leaves out|
|---|---|---|
|Module 23 (v30): hook architecture|A hook specification in four terms (place, melodic feature, words, compound channels), five hook types, the approach (a withheld resolution of two bars or more, a held approach note, a build), a four-step prosody audit, six strength indicators (four needed)|The indicators come from the literature and were never tested in the engine|
|Window 17 (v30): memory and hook science|Earworms, the unfinished phrase, the anticipation and arrival reward, phrase endings as memory anchors|A review, with no measurement|
|Module 4 (v44): the motif detector|Four-note motifs (contour and rhythm) that return exactly or varied; real verse and chorus pairs score a median of 0.79|Weak against hits (AUC 0.52); says nothing about recall|
|Window 42 (v56): the money note|Under the title's last content word the chord is I 37%, IV 22%, V 17%; the chorus peak is on an unstable degree 40% of the time; listeners' arousal rises at peak notes|Arousal, not memory|
|Window 45 (v57): convergence|In 97 rated hits arousal climbs with the number of convergence elements at a bar|Arousal, not memory|
|Window 48 (v61): the earworm profile|Jakubowski's three earworm features measured on 12,163 choruses; demoted after AUC 0.48 to 0.51 against the chart|Tested against sales, not against being stuck in the head|
|Windows 62 and 63 (v79): survival and description length|Survival among hits close to unpredictable (concordance 0.531); compressibility null|The hook's own outcome, said to be out of reach|
|Module 10.20 (v89): the quotable line|Ranks a song's lines against each other; the writer's blind picks are the label|Words only, not the tune|
|Module 27.4 and v63: title-first design, the refrain kernel|The title's cell copied where it ends chorus lines; hooks aimed at a stressed full vowel|Where the title goes and how often is not drawn from data|

### What the recent songs needed

Songs 52 to 56 had their hooks set by design questions or by sketch, and v7 checked them. Nothing could tell the engine whether one candidate hook is stickier than another. Finding 749.8 keeps each hook exact while inner chorus lines vary, so the hook is also the one part of a song that must not drift.

## 2. The academic record

The studies that measured memory itself point away from Module 23's "unusual interval". The sections people recognise fastest have the voice up front, sound typical of pop, and repeat within the song. Distinctiveness helps in one narrow way: a rare cell makes a passage feel familiar, even when it is new.

### Catchiness measured as recognition

Burgoyne and colleagues defined a hook as the most salient, easiest-to-recall fragment of a song, and catchiness as long-term musical salience. Their game Hooked drops the needle at the start of a section and times how fast players recognise the song ([Burgoyne et al. 2013)](https://zenodo.org/records/1417599). The Dutch game logged 167,704 responses from 1,986 players. The UK version, Hooked on Music, drew over 160,000 players and over 3 million responses on 1,000 excerpts from 200 chart-toppers [(Van Balen 2016, ch. 7)](https://jvbalen.github.io/pdf/thesis-CH7.pdf).

|Study|Data|What made a section recognisable|
|---|---|---|
|[Van Balen et al. 2015;](https://zenodo.org/records/1415038) [thesis ch. 8](https://jvbalen.github.io/pdf/thesis-CH8.pdf)|1,715 sections of 321 songs, 973 players; 99 songs transcribed|Vocal prominence, the strongest (+0.14 per SD); a typical sound, melody, harmony and range (+0.05 to +0.09); melodic repetitiveness (+0.12); typical motifs (+0.07). No support for distinctiveness. Between-song differences were 37% to 40% of the variance|
|[Korsmit et al. 2017](https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/16325081/Korsmit_et_al.pdf)|Hooked on Music, 4,082 players, 184 fragments|Listener differences: female vocals from 2006 to 2013, songs of the listener's teens (1990s), a rap and beat factor; one factor for fragments easy to sing along with|
|[Schulkind et al. 2003](https://esf.ccarh.org/254-old/254_LiteraturePack1/MelFeatures4_MelID(Schulkind).pdf)|34 familiar songs, played note by note|Named by about the 6th note (mean 6.35). Helped by phrase boundaries, long notes (over a beat), the first beat of the bar, the first note of a repeated pair, a completed up-down alternation. Pitch height and interval size did not matter|
|[Dalla Bella et al. 2003, via Filipic et al. 2010](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.3758/PBR.17.3.335.pdf)|Familiar songs on piano|Familiar after about 4 notes (2.3 s), sure after about 6 (3.1 s). From the real recording, half a second can be enough|
|[Jakubowski et al. 2017](https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/1371487)|100 earworm tunes against 100 matched|A more common overall contour; less common gradients between turning points; tempo 124 against 116 bpm (a trend). How popular and how recent the song was mattered more|
|[Müllensiefen and Halpern 2014](https://eprints-gro.gold.ac.uk/10838/1/PSY-Mu%CC%88llensiefen2014.pdf)|80 pop phrases, unfamiliar to the listeners|Rare motifs (against the other test phrases) gave more correct recognitions; rare motifs against the pop corpus gave more false "I've heard it"|
|[Sonic logos](https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/items/903c50f3-6d66-4721-af94-7c037073b139) (Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts)|90 brand logos, 1,860 listeners|Complexity helped recognition and hurt singing it back|

### What listeners carry away

- **The chorus.** It is the section most often reported stuck in the head, and pieces with vocals are about twice as likely to be ([Liptak et al. 2022,](https://research.gold.ac.uk/30547/16/mp.2022.39.3.320.pdf) citing Beaman and Williams, Liikkanen, and Floridou).

- **Exposure first.** Tempo and lyrics shape earworms only through what the listener habitually hears (Liptak et al. 2022). Popularity and recency outweighed the melody in Jakubowski's data.

- **Singing along.** In 1,054 song events in English pubs, context explained about 40% of sing-along and the music about another 25%, vocal performance above all ([Pawley and Müllensiefen 2012)](https://research.gold.ac.uk/9009).

- **Repetition sells.** In 2,480 Hot 100 songs, each extra chorus repetition raised the odds of a number one by 14.5% [(Nunes, Ordanini and Valsesia 2015, as reported](https://tonedeaf.thebrag.com/?p=430020)).

**Recognisable is catchy.** In ratings of 54 excerpts, recognisability raised catchiness strongly (B = 0.29), and catchiness went with the urge to move (ρ ≈ 0.49) [(Bechtold, Curry and Witek 2025)](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1642561/full).

### What this means

Recognition and recall pull apart. A hook has to be recognised in a few notes and also sung back. The research says: put the voice on it, keep its frame typical, repeat it, land it on long notes and strong beats at a phrase boundary, and give it one rare cell. Module 23's six indicators reward an unusual interval and an arch, which is half of that.

## 3. New vectors found in appendices, bibliographies and arXiv

Following the reference lists and appendices opened eleven lines of work that v7 does not have. Three are used in this study; the rest are listed for v8 and later studies.

|Vector|Where it came from|What it adds|Here|
|---|---|---|---|
|Song-based and corpus-based typicality|Van Balen et al. 2015, built on FANTASTIC (Müllensiefen 2009)|Two different measures: how much a section repeats its own song, and how common its cells are across all songs|Used (self-repetition, typical cells)|
|The cohort model of melody recognition|Schulkind et al. 2003, citing Marslen- Wilson's spoken-word model; Dalla Bella et al. 2003; [Thiesen, Kopiez and Müllensiefen 2020](https://research.gold.ac.uk/id/eprint/29012/)|A melody is identified when its opening stops matching other songs, around notes 5 to 7; section, duration, voice and orderliness change speed|Used (notes until unique)|
|The fastest-recognised list|Hooked on Music's published top 20 with recognition times ( [as reported](https://csmonitor.com/Science/2014/1101/Catchiest-song-of-all-time-A-Spice-Girls-tune-say-British-scientists))|An outcome for hooks, not sales|Used (14 songs)|
|Recognition against sung recall|[Sonic logos study;](https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/items/903c50f3-6d66-4721-af94-7c037073b139) Müllensiefen and Halpern 2014; [Silas and Müllensiefen 2023](https://research.gold.ac.uk/id/eprint/34398)|Complexity helps recognition and hurts singing back; length is the main limit on learning a tune|A two-sided test for v8|
|A rare cell feels familiar|Müllensiefen and Halpern 2014, citing Rhodes and Castel 2009|One distinctive motif makes a new song feel already known|A rule for v8|
|Listener differences|Korsmit et al. 2017, citing Krumhansl and Zupnick 2013 on reminiscence bumps|What is recognised depends on the listener's age and the singer's sex|An audience row at intake|
|Catchiness and groove|[Bechtold, Curry and Witek 2025](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1642561/full) and their 2023 and 2024 studies|Catchiness in 1 second and in 10 seconds are different; both go with the urge to move|Ties the hook to Part 10's rhythm layer|
|YouTube's "most replayed" graph|arXiv: [Rhapsody (2505.19429),](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19429v1) [YTMR500 (2309.06102),](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06102v1) [Mr. HiSum](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/file/7f880e3a325b06e3601af1384a653038-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks.pdf)|A replay curve in 100 steps for most videos with 50,000 views or more: a moment-by-moment listener outcome for millions of songs|Not reachable from this workspace; the strongest next study|
|Memorability of unfamiliar music|arXiv [2405.12847](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12847v1) (ISMIR 2023, YTMM)|Recall of instrumental intros after a delay; higher valence, arousal and tempo helped|Background|
|Repetition structure and hook detection|arXiv [2209.00182](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.00182) (over half of POP909 phrases repeat at once); [2410.19540](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.19540) (expert hook labels); [2205.14700](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14700) (verse and chorus from audio)|Tools to mark hooks in real recordings and in our demos|For the demo check|
|Hookpad Aria|arXiv [2502.08122](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.08122v1)|Hooktheory's own melody assistant: 318,000 suggestions, 74,000 accepted by users|A preference signal, if its logs were ever shared|

One more vector is a request, not a search. The full Hooked on Music data (over 3 million responses on 1,000 excerpts) was never released. It would test every claim in this study on real recognition times. The team is at the University of Amsterdam (Burgoyne, Music Cognition Group); asking them for it is worth one email.

## 4. Measured: hooks in our corpora

Three measurements, and one result stands above the rest. The choruses players recognised fastest are built from common cells and plain intervals. Our songs 54 to 56 have choruses that repeat their own cells less than about 90% of real choruses.

Chorus against verse in the same song

Hooktheory gives 22,407 transcribed sections of 16 notes or more, with their section names. In 2,839 songs with both a chorus and a verse, each chorus was compared with its own verse (studies/hooks, hooks_analyse.py).

|Measure|Chorus higher in|Median difference|
|---|---|---|
|Mean pitch|67% of songs|+1.5 semitones|
|Self-repetition (share of the section's 3- to 5-note cells heard again in it)|56%|+0.03|
|Surprise (bits per note, model trained on other songs)|54%|+0.06|
|Typical cells (how many other songs share each cell)|46%|slightly less typical|
|Notes per beat|47%|−0.02|
|Notes until the opening is unique to the song|no difference||

The chorus is mainly higher. It is only a little more repetitive than its verse, and no more typical. So what makes a chorus the part people carry away is mostly not in its intervals: it is the voice, the register, the words and how often it comes round.

The other sections each have a job. Intros, where instrumental hooks live, are the most repetitive part of the song: against the verse (1,026 songs) they repeat more in 64% and their main cell covers more of the notes in 71%. Pre-choruses (871 songs) sit higher than the verse in 64% but repeat less (37%) and surprise more (57%). Bridges (665 songs) repeat less than the chorus (41%) and surprise more (57%).

Inside a chorus, the most frequent 4-note cell returns a median of 3 times (middle half 2 to 4). It is first heard in the opening quarter of the chorus in 88% of choruses and covers a quarter of its notes.

Openings become unique to their song quickly when rhythm counts: by the 6th note in about half of choruses and by the 8th in 86%. By intervals alone, only 8% are unique by the 6th note and 39% by the 8th. That matches Schulkind's finding that rhythm and long notes, not pitch, drive identification.

### The songs players recognised fastest

![Fastest-recognised choruses use common cells and plain intervals](data:image/png;base64,)

studies/hooks: hooks_catchiest.py (14 of the 20 songs Hooked on Music players recognised fastest, published November 2014) and hooks_our_songs.py

Fifteen of the 20 published fastest-recognised songs are in Hooktheory, 14 with chorus transcriptions. Their choruses sit at the 81st percentile for typical cells (11 of 14 above the median, p = 0.057), the 27th for surprise and the 33rd for interval variety (12 of 14 below, p = 0.013). Their openings also take longer than most to become unique (12 of 14, p = 0.013). Self-repetition and the main cell's share are ordinary. Fourteen songs is a small sample, but the direction is Van Balen's: recognisable means typical.

### Where the title goes

CoCoPops transcribes 214 Billboard hits (1958 to 1991) with their sung syllables (hooks_titles.py; lines read from punctuation, rests of 3/4 beat or more and section changes). The title is sung in 156 of them.

|Measure|Result|
|---|---|
|Times the title is sung|median 8 (middle half 4 to 12)|
|Songs with a chorus that sing the title in it|87% of 134|
|Where the title is sung|chorus 57%, verse 22%, outro and fade 11%|
|Choruses carrying the title|82% of 375; median 2 times each (75th percentile 3), in a third of the lines|
|Place in the chorus|first line 40% (chance 33%), last line 28%, the very first word 27%|
|Rhythm|starts on a beat 73%, on beat 1 33%; its notes held 1.33 times the song's median note, the longest 2 times|
|Pitch|on the section's top note 31%|
|First heard|median 39 s (middle half 16 to 60 s), 18% of the way in|

The title opens the chorus more often than it closes it. The songwriting habit of saving the title for the last line is the minority case in these hits.

### Songs 52 to 56

Each section was measured as a Hooktheory clip is and placed against clips of the same kind and similar length (hooks_our_songs.py, hooks_our_titles.py). Percentiles:

|Song|Self-repetition|Interval variety|Typical cells|Surprise|Title|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|52, chorus|1|48|40|60|sung 3 times, first at 38 s|
|53, refrain|6|50|83|93|not read|
|54, chorus|6|68|35|53|full title 3 times, first at 116 s (47% in); its key words in every chorus|
|55, chorus|2|74|49|49|7 times, first at 41 s, opening every chorus|
|56, chorus|5|90|27|74|never sung; the chorus's own phrase twice in each|

Every chorus repeats its own cells less than at least 94% of real choruses its length. In songs 54 to 56 the verse repeats more than the chorus (percentiles 16 against 6, 42 against 2, 75 against 5), the reverse of the norm. Song 56's chorus is the furthest from the fastest-recognised profile: high variety, less typical cells, above-median surprise.

## 5. What v8 should do

v8 should score hooks for recognition, not novelty: a typical frame, a chorus that repeats itself, the title placed where hits place it, and one fresh note where the voice comes back. Each rule below has a check that runs on every song. If they go on the fix list, they would be findings 749.24 onward.

### H1. Rewrite Module 23's strength indicators

|Now (23.6)|Replace with|Why|
|---|---|---|
|An unusual interval at the turning point (high weight)|The chorus's cells at or above the 60th percentile of chorus typicality (aim for the 75th), its interval variety and surprise per note at or below the median|Van Balen 2015; the 14 fastest-recognised choruses sit at the 81st, 33rd and 27th percentiles|
|(none)|One fresh note per hook phrase, placed at the re-entry after a breath|Part 9 and finding 749.19; Müllensiefen and Halpern 2014 (a rare cell feels familiar)|
|A common arch or descent (medium)|Kept, as a report only|Jakubowski 2017; Window 48|
|Compound hook, approach, prosody, cadence|Kept|Byron et al. 2025; the pre-chorus corpus result below|

### H2. The chorus repeats itself

**Rule:** the chorus's self-repetition sits at or above the median of real choruses its length, and above its own verse. Its main 4-note cell returns at least 3 times (real choruses: median 3, middle half 2 to 4), first inside the opening quarter, covering about a quarter of the notes.

- **How:** the chorus's lines share a rhythm cell (lines 1 and 3, or 1 and 2, sung to the same cell), the way v63's cell grammar already copies the refrain kernel.

- **Why it matters now:** songs 52 to 56 sit at the 1st to 6th percentile, and in songs 54 to 56 the verse repeats more than the chorus.

- **Check:** hooks_our_songs.py on every pick.

### H3. The title

- In the chorus (87% of hits with a chorus), about twice in each chorus (75th percentile 3), about 8 times in the song (flag under 4).

- In the chorus's first line more often than its last (40% against 28%); first heard by about 40 seconds (middle half 16 to 60 s).

- On a beat (73%), its notes held longer than the song's median note (1.3 times; the longest twice). The top note is optional (31%).

- A song whose hook phrase is not its title (song 56) applies these to the hook phrase and prints where the title falls.

### H4. Identity through rhythm

The hook's opening should become unique to the song by its 8th note when rhythm is counted (86% of real choruses), while its intervals stay common (only 39% are unique by intervals alone). Long notes and downbeats at the phrase boundary carry identification (Schulkind et al. 2003). Check: the uniqueness point against the Hooktheory index, at or under 8 notes.

### H5. Each section keeps its job

|Section|Corpus result (against the verse unless noted)|v8 target|
|---|---|---|
|Intro|The most repetitive part: main cell covers more in 71% of songs|An instrumental hook built from one repeated cell (with Part 25 and v7's instrumental hook)|
|Pre-chorus|Higher in 64%, repeats less in 63%, surprises more in 57%|The approach: rising, less settled (Module 23.4 confirmed)|
|Chorus|Higher in 67%, repeats a little more in 56%|H1 to H4|
|Bridge|Repeats less than the chorus in 59%, surprises more in 57%|Contrast, as Part 18 says|

### H6. Recognise it and sing it back

A hook must pass two tests that pull against each other: recognition (helped by one distinctive cell) and singing back (hurt by complexity and length). The hook phrase stays inside one breath and one phrase (the memory ceiling of about 8 seconds, Part 11), repeats, and keeps its one fresh note. The voice carries it: vocal prominence was the strongest predictor of recognition, so the mix keeps the lead on top at every hook (Module 9.12's stems rule).

### Tests for v8

1. Songs 52 to 56 rerun: every chorus at or above the 50th length-matched percentile for self-repetition and the 60th for typical cells, interval variety at or below the 50th.

2. Title rules H3 pass, or the exception is printed.

3. Uniqueness point at or under 8 notes with rhythm counted.

4. Finding 749.8's varied repeats still leave the hook and first line exact.

5. A blind A/B with Jason: the v7 pick against the H1 to H4 pick for one song, his choice logged.

## 6. Files and sources

In the repo (studies/hooks)

- hooks_hooktheory.py: features of 22,407 Hooktheory sections (self-repetition, typical cells, surprise, the main cell, uniqueness points); writes hooks_clips.json (derived numbers only)

- hooks_analyse.py: chorus against verse, intro, pre-chorus and bridge in the same song; hooks_hooktheory_results.json

- hooks_catchiest.py: the 14 fastest-recognised songs against all choruses; hooks_catchiest_results.json

- hooks_titles.py: where titles fall in 214 CoCoPops hits; hooks_titles_results.json (no lyrics kept)

- hooks_our_songs.py and hooks_our_titles.py: songs 52 to 56; hooks_our_songs.json, hooks_our_titles.json
